Barcelona, Spain. * Corresponding author: hael1790@gmail.com Abstract S The use of color in audiovisual projects, specifically film, tv, and advertising involves associations at different levels: physical, psychological, and aesthetic. To our knoSwledge, the specific impact of pastel colors on viewers had not been studied by comparing them tEo saturated colors based on paired color productions. In this work, we aimed to approach differencesR in the emotions perceived by viewers when watching audiovisual projects produced with pastel colors compared with the production with saturated P colors. We hypothesized that the pastel color, due to its characteristic of being a soft color, evokes emotions with less intensity than saturated colors. To study this, we created 12 videos, six with a saturated color N production design and six with a pastel color production design, evoking six basic emotions: disgust, anger, I fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise. We presented these videos to 310 people distributed in two groups (half of them watched the saturated videos aEnd half the pastel videos) and asked them to indicate how these six emotions were evoked. We only found significant differences in 4 out of the 36 comparisons made L (11.11%), in videos representing disgust and anger. With those results, we did not find that pastel color in C audiovisual projects clearly influences audience’s emotional perception. We conclude that to evoke I emotions in the audience, more additional elements to color are necessary, such as music, camera shots or T lighting. This research brings more knowledge to how pastel color in images, particularly those of an R audiovisual nature, can be used to evoke emotions in the audience. ARTICLE IN PRESS INTRODUCTION Color plays a central role in audiovisual storytelling, shaping the viewer’s perception, emotional response, and interpretation of scenes (Bordwell et al., 2016). In film, television, and advertising, color is carefully chosen to support narrative tone, guide attention, and elicit specific psychological reactions (Block, 2008; Kaiser, 1996). While considerable research has explored how saturated or contrasting colors in audiovisuals influence emotions (Baumgärtner et al. 2016; Codispoti et al., 2012; Cowan, 2015; İyilikci et al., 2024; Kennedy, 2014; Martínez et al., 2012; Sánchez-Alarcón, 2008), far less is known about the emotional impact of softer hues—particularly pastel colors—within the context of audiovisual production. This paper addresses that gap by examining whether pastel colors modulate emotional perception in audiovisual projects. The study of color in audiovisuals Color in audiovisual projects (film, TV, advertising) has not been studied enough in a scientific setting (Cotes, 2010; Elliot, 2015, 2016; Everret, 2007; Peacock, 2010), although it influences the way in which the audience perceives audiovisual projects (Ikeda, 2020; Pressey, 1921; Shimamura, 2013). Each color S carries symbolic meaning based on its historical associations, which audiovisual producers use to influence S viewers' subconscious and perception of the frame (Flückiger, 2017). In film, for example, color contributes to shaping atmosphere, mood, and provides additional context abEout the narrative and characters. It fulfills plot-related, dramatic, and symbolic functions within a comRplementary color scheme (Dziuba & Kovsh, 2022). P Color serves multiple functions in audiovisual Nwork. Physically, it may affect viewer comfort; psychologically, it can elicit emotional responses; and aesthetically, it contributes to visual balance, I proportion, and composition (Cao et al., 2024; Zhang, 2024). Empirical studies support these roles: for example, color film sequences generally reEceive higher valence ratings than black-and-white sequences (Cao et al., 2024), and color images are fLound more exciting than monochrome ones in television viewing (Detenber, Simons, & Reiss, 2000). Additionally, emotions can mediate cross-modal association between C music and visual color (Lindborg & Friberg, 2015). Recognizing this, audiovisual creators increasingly use I color not only to enrich aesthetic experience but also to enhance drama, describe characters, and convey T mood and emotion—strengthening its position as a vital narrative device (Braga & Vaz Da Costa, 2011). R The perception of colorA and the role of context Color is one of the fundamental properties used to identify objects, alongside size and texture (Bianconi et al., 2021). Because of this, it plays a significant role in perceptual processing (Folk, 2015). Numerous studies have demonstrated the emotional effects of color stimuli (Wilms & Oberfeld, 2018). For instance, color temperature and illuminance can influence emotional states, physiological responses, and productivity (Chen, Tsai, & Tsay, 2022); hue preference has been linked to gender and cultural background (Al-Rasheed, 2015); and saturation levels can alter perceived object size (Hagtvedt & Brasel, 2017). Saturated and bright colors are associated with higher arousal (Wilms and Oberfeld, 2018); colors are associated with tastes and flavors (Spence, 2019) and emotional tones—for instance, yellow is linked with joy, yellow-green with relaxation (Jonauskaite et al., 2019), green is associated with environmental friendliness, and grey evokes environmental unfriendliness (Lim et al., 2020). So, the use of the color can enhance the narrative by manipulating intent and improving message delivery (Čerepinko et al., 2023). However, to fully understand color’s effect, researchers must also consider its embodied and referential associations, as well as properties like hue and saturation (Lim et al., 2020). These perceptual and symbolic layers are critical when analyzing emotional responses to color. Research shows that color associations are relatively consistent across studies, although often limited by the range of colors and emotions analyzed (Hanada, 2017). The impact of these associations depends ARTICLE IN PRESS heavily on context, particularly in terms of embodied meanings—linked to biological responses—and referential meanings—linked to learned associations shaped by cultural background and usage (Labrecque et al., 2013). While cultural factors can influence these associations, some intrinsic perceptions of color appear to be shared globally. Therefore, context plays a determining role in activating certain associations within the semantic network and influencing perception and behavior (Labrecque et al., 2013). Various theoretical interpretations of color perception have been proposed over the decades (Heller, 2008; Kalmus, 1935; Plutchik, 2001; Wells, 1910). Although consensus is lacking on the precise emotional effects of specific colors—or even how to name them (Uusküla et al., 2023)—some general patterns are widely accepted. For instance, red is commonly associated with danger, passion, and aggression; green with balance and respect; and blue with authority and melancholy (Edwards, 2004). Research shows that red in audiovisual scenes sustains tension, green conveys harmony, and blue emphasizes calm and communication (Čerepinko et al., 2023). Directors often select colors based not only on general associations but also personal interpretations to convey tone, mood, and character, making color one of the most influential elements in shaping audience emotion (Dziuba & Kovsh, 2022). S An example of the recognition of color potential by audiovisual producers can be seen in green marketing S where green is used to signal environmental friendliness, particularly in advertising, packaging, and branding strategies (Lim et al., 2020). This can create emotional rEesonance, but misuse (as in greenwashing) can backfire. Similarly, experimental studies show that viewRers respond emotionally to color cues even before identifying the actual content—for instance, associating red backgrounds with anger and green P backgrounds with happiness in emoticons (Ikeda, 2020). Supporting this, Jonauskaite et al. (2019) found that positive moods are linked to light and chromaNtic colors, while negative moods correspond to dark, achromatic ones. Marketing research further supports that effective use of color enhances emotional I engagement and brand loyalty, depending on visual harmony and cultural symbolism (Martínez et al., 2012). E L Although these findings are significant, many researchers emphasize the need for further study to clarify C how specific colors evoke emotional responses, especially in multimedia contexts (Fetterman et al., 2015; I Jalil et al., 2012; Jonauskaite et al., 2020; Oittinen et al., 2015). The current study contributes to this area T by exploring the emotional effects of pastel colors in audiovisual content. R A Pastel color The human eye perceives colors based on hue, saturation, and brightness (Krantz, 1972). Among these, pastel colors are characterized by lower chromatic intensity and higher luminance while retaining the original hue (Cajal, 2020; Chittick, 1980). Subjectively, they are described as soft and soothing (Arrarte- Grau, 2016). As saturation decreases, a color becomes pastel rather than vivid. Pastel tones are softer than primary colors (Fordham & Hayes, 2009) and have been used since the sixteenth century by artists for their expressiveness and subtlety (Yang & Min, 2017). Commonly seen in commercial design, pastel colors are associated with simplicity, beauty, cleanliness, spring, summer, and relaxation (Abbasi et al., 2014; Kroeger et al., 1986; Zviran, Dov Te’eni, & Gross, 2006). Mulyati and Exposto (2023), for instance, found that colors like light green, light blue, and light yellow create calming and cheerful environments in pediatric spaces, although pink may increase anxiety. As in Ecological Valence Theory, which proposes that people’s color preferences are shaped by their associations with objects or experiences they like or dislike (Palmer & Schloss, 2010), pastel tones are believed to affect consumers emotionally and intellectually (Casas & Chinoperekweyi, 2019), and their acceptance is influenced by cultural and functional norms—such as professional dress codes that favor neutral colors. Yet, despite the ubiquity of pastel colors in visual culture, the emotional impact of them within audiovisual storytelling remains underexplored. ARTICLE IN PRESS The present study In this context, to our knowledge, the specific impact of pastel colors on viewers had not previously been studied in a manner based on paired color productions, such as comparing pastel to saturated colors. We hypothesized that pastel colors, due to their soft nature, evoke basic emotions with less intensity, —that is, weaker or milder emotional responses, both positive and negative—compared to saturated colors. To test this, we created 12 videos—six with a saturated color design and six with a pastel color design, using the type of color as independent variable—each intended to primarily evoke one of six basic emotions: disgust, anger, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise (Ekman, 1999, 2003). These videos were shown to participants, divided into two groups (half viewing the saturated videos and half viewing the pastel videos), and they were asked to rate the intensity of the six emotions elicited by each video. We analyzed the intensity of each of the studied emotions as dependent variables across both conditions (saturated and pastel videos) to address our research question: how does pastel color in audiovisuals modulate viewers’ emotional responses? METHODS S S Participants In total, 310 subjects (205 women, 95 men and 10 preferred noEt to indicate), distributed in two groups, participated in this study: 155 participants were part of the pRastel group, and 155 participants were part of the saturated color group. We randomly distributed our participants between both groups of this study. The P age of the participants was distributed as follows: 183 were between 18-24 years old; 42 were 25-34 years old; 23 were 35-44 years old; 33 were 45-54 years Nold; and 29 were 55 or older. Since 72 out of the 310 participants did not answer all the parameters, we got some data loss, but 77% of participants answered the I complete study. We used all the available data from participants who did not complete the entire questionnaire. The experiment was carried oEut in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations for human research and the protocol was appLroved by the Ethics Commission for Research with Animals and Humans (CEEAH) of the Universitat C Autònoma de Barcelona (Barcelona, Spain), with CEEAH reference number 6048. I T Stimuli and Pre-tests R We created 12 videos, each designed to primarily promote one of Paul Ekman’s basic six emotions (disgust, anger, fear, happiness, sAadness, and surprise) (Ekman, 1999, 2003) in two color production approaches (pastel color and saturated color). It is important to note that our goal was not to create ‘pure’ emotional stimuli but rather to understand how pastel versus saturated colors influence the perceived intensity of dominant emotions, even when other secondary emotions may be present. Emotional stimuli in real audiovisual productions are rarely pure; mixed emotional responses are common in naturalistic settings (Gabert-Quillen et al., 2015; Harold, 2010; Singh et al., 2021). The stories that happened in the videos were the following: (1) surprise: a male character arrives disappointed to his house to be surprised by his female partner; (2) disgust: a couple eat pasta in a very disgusting way; (3) anger: a male character gets irritated while speaking with a customer service representative over the phone; (4) happiness: a male character relaxes on his bedroom imagining her female partner in lovely situations; (5) fear: a male character shaves his bear in his bathroom when suddenly his dead female partner jumps out and scares him; and (6) sadness: a male character is sleeping with his female partner, when he wakes up and returns to sleep to realize his partner is dead. Each video promoting each emotion had two versions: one with pastel colors and one with saturated colors. Both versions shared the same narrative, the same characters, the same scenarios, the same duration (30 seconds), but a different color production. The color production was approached in the production phase rather than postproduction. Thus, we recorded 12 videos in total (Figure 1). To confirm that the video evoked the intended emotion, we conducted two pre-tests. ARTICLE IN PRESS Pre-test 1 involved the initial versions of the 12 videos, where participants were asked to identify the emotion conveyed and the color scheme of the video. A total of 78 participants completed this online pre- test over a one-week period. To ensure the accuracy of our stimuli, we set a threshold that at least 85% of participants had to agree that each video evoked the predetermined emotion. The results indicated that only the pastel sadness and saturated fear videos met this criterion. The remaining videos (pastel surprise, saturated surprise, pastel disgust, saturated disgust, pastel anger, saturated anger, pastel joy, saturated joy, pastel fear, and saturated sadness) did not meet the 85% threshold. As a result, we developed Pre-test 2, where we revised the videos based on the feedback from Pre-test 1. To further validate the changes, we sought professional opinions from six screenwriters and academics. These experts reviewed the rewritten scripts, based on the pre-test results, and provided feedback on how to enhance the scripts to better evoke the intended emotions. The final scripts incorporated their suggestions, and the videos were re-recorded to ensure they accurately conveyed the desired emotional responses. After the final stimuli were produced, we confirmed their effectiveness in eliciting the intended emotions by analyzing participants’ responses in the main study. We checked that the desired emotion for each video scored higher on the corresponding Likert scale. S S We used Highland2 for writing the scripts and DaVinci Resolve 17 for editing the videos. Each group of participants watched a group of six videos in either pastel color oEr saturated color. One version presented the pastel videos, and the other version presented the saturated videos. We understood that a Likert scale was the I best asset to measure the impact of emotional elicitation since research aimed to evaluate the effectiveness T of a Likert scale as a tool for measuring basic emotions and understanding their intensity in different R contexts has been proven adequate (Nicoara et al., 2023). A We used Random.org for randomizing the presentation of the videos in each group (pastel group and saturated group). The aim of the study was for the participants to see each video and determine the level of emotion evoked in each one of them. The studies were online distributed between December 8th, 2022, and March 5th, 2023. We posted the links to both versions of the study from Forms.app to a mailing list of students and professors from the Universidad del Sagrado Corazón in Puerto Rico and to mailing list provided by the Puerto Rico European Film Festival and the Puerto Rico Documentary Filmmakers Association. The links to the studies were also handled in-person to students of the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona in Spain and the Universidad del Sagrado Corazón in Puerto Rico. Data analysis We used participants’ answers to the studies for the analysis. To approach distribution, we applied Shapiro Wilk normality test (p < .05). We did multivariate tests, analysis of variances and unpaired t-tests to the data or its equivalent non-parametric Mann-Whitney test. We compared the impact that color condition (pastel versus saturated) may have in viewers’ emotions. For each video, we analyzed, not only the target emotion (e.g., in disgust video, disgust emotion), but also the rest of the acquired emotions to check if, in any case, the color condition would have a significant impact on viewers’ emotions. We used JASP and Sigmaplot for statistical analysis. ARTICLE IN PRESS RESULTS In the present study, we aimed to answer if pastel color would impact in viewers’ emotions compared with saturated color. Initially a MANOVA Wilks’ test was performed to analyze the effect of the type of color [color condition: pastel color or saturated color] would have on the type of emotion [emotion condition: disgust, anger, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise] on the rating of participants in the Likert scale to the stimuli. There was non-significant difference in rating the emotions based on color condition (F = (1,1375) 0.906, p = .906, Wilk's Λ = .998). R P [FIGURE 7 HERE] N I DISCUSSION E The aim of this work was to study the imLpact that pastel color could have on viewers’ emotions, compared to saturated colors. We hypothesizeCd that pastel color would evoke emotions with less intensity than saturated colors. The analysis of all the data together showed non-significant differences in viewers’ I emotions based on the color condition. When looking at the data in detail, our findings revealed significant T differences in only 4 out of the 36 comparisons made (11.11%), specifically in videos representing disgust R and anger, where pastel color production resulted in a less intense emotional response in only three of the A cases. In the case of the disgust video, the emotions that presented significant differences were happiness and fear, with a lower impact of them in the pastel videos. In the case of the anger video, the emotions that provoked different emotional responses were happiness and sadness, with a lower level of the emotion in pastel condition in the case of happiness. So, these modest differences suggest that pastel color in audiovisual projects does not significantly influence the audience's emotional perception on its own. Note that while each video was designed to primarily evoke a specific target emotion (e.g., disgust, anger), we analyzed participants’ responses across all six basic emotions for each video. This approach allowed us to explore whether pastel colors decreased emotional intensity broadly, regardless of whether the emotional response matched the video’s target emotion. Previous research on color-emotion associations shows that primary saturated colors like red, green, yellow, purple, and blue evoke stronger emotions than intermediate and achromatic colors (Kaya & Epps, 2004). Our study reveals that pastel colors do not impact in a solid way in emotional response compared to saturated colors. Many previous empirical works have proven that, in audiovisual projects, light (Matbouly, 2022), diegetic and non-diegetic sound such as explosions or gunshots (Shimamura, 2013), surround sound (Langiulli et al., 2023), music (Hunter & Schellenberg, 2010), cuts (Andreu-Sánchez et al., 2022) or style of editing (Andreu-Sánchez et al., 2018) among many others, impact viewers’ perception and/or emotions. ARTICLE IN PRESS Color in audiovisual projects has previously been linked to emotions (Kennedy, 2014), but it seems that saturation of color, or even removing color information from audiovisual projects, has only a slight influence on them: research by Codispoti et al. (2012) has shown that color information in audiovisual stimuli does not necessarily influence emotional responses. Their study found that removing color did not affect the emotional processing of natural scenes, regardless of exposure duration, suggesting that recognizing the emotional content of scenes does not heavily depend on color. Similar findings were found by İyilikci and colleagues (İyilikci et al., 2024) regarding the use of color to elicit emotions. In their studies they aimed to investigate the potential effects of sound and color in film clips on emotion-elicitation levels. The researchers found that color had a smaller impact on self-reported feelings compared to sound in response to film clips. Removing color only slightly affected emotions causing a minor decrease in sadness ratings and a slight increase in anger ratings within their respective categories. These results, along with ours, makes us think that color may not have such an important impact on viewers’ emotions. Another observation İyilikci and colleagues (İyilikci et al., 2024) found about color was that the color versions of calm or neutral film clips elicited higher levels of pleasantness. In contrast, the black-and-white versions of these clips tended to evoke more boredom and confusion. Given that the calmness category mostly features daylight nature scenes, it’s expected that colors like blue, green, or bright hues are linked to positive S emotions (İyilikci et al., 2024). On this regard, color impacts differently based on the type of content S represented: while removing color from portraits increases perception of pleasantness and beauty and reduces tension, removing color from landscapes reduces the peErception of beauty (Polzella, Hammar & Hinkle, 2005). R P In a study made with humans and monkeys, it was proven that color cues have different impact in the task of categorization depending on the type of object tNhat must be recognized (Delorme, Richard, & Fabre- Thorpe, 2000). These observations are relevant to our results since we found that the content of the video I have more impact on viewers’ emotion than the type of color (pastel versus saturated) itself. E Another study (Kuzinas et al., 2016) set toL find correlations between hue and content to trigger an emotional response in the audience showed that natural scenes evoked more positive and less arousing emotions C compared to urban scenes. Green images were less arousing than red ones, and original images triggered I the most pleasant emotions. Notably, green was the only hue where the emotional impact of the content T was evident. Natural scenes paired with green elicited more positive emotions than urban scenes paired R with green. These results are interconnected and can be understood within the framework of cognitive fluency meaning that whAen something is easy to understand, recognize, or process, it tends to evoke more positive emotions and perceptions. In the context of our results, there may be no difference in the experience of processing content with saturated colors versus with pastel colors. Not taking color in consideration we could argue that by working on the script, on the production, the acting, and the sound, media creators can achieve the desired emotions. İyilikci and colleagues (İyilikci et al., 2024) found that sound-enhanced film clips were more effective at evoking target emotions compared to their silent counterparts. These results, which show small to moderate effect sizes, align with the notion that sound, particularly background music, contributes additively to the emotional experience, given that the visual content already elicits a strong emotional response (İyilikci et al., 2024). Following a similar line of research, a study using the effectiveness of different aspect ratios instead of sound to elicit emotions found that mid-wide aspects ratios like (16:9) elicit higher emotional response compared to standard (4:3) and ultra-wide (21:9 aspect ratios. This demonstrate that designing features within an audiovisual project can have emotional effects when determining emotional reactions in viewers (Kuzinas et al., 2024). This is consistent with previous studies such as those of Arthur Shimamura (2013) or Noël Carroll and William Seeley (2013), which emphasize the primordial need for an intention on the part of audiovisual makers to evoke emotions over any practical element in audiovisual production. Lingzhie Nie (2021) argue that the development of the connoted meanings of colors is related to the development of the spiritual and material culture of each linguistic community and, therefore, reflects each culture. Color preferences are closely ARTICLE IN PRESS linked to the emotions they evoke, with certain colors consistently eliciting positive or negative feelings. Although some colors are universally preferred across different ages, racial groups, and cultures, there is evidence suggesting that color preferences can also be influenced by cultural factors (Kaya & Epps, 2004). Since the values associated with colors vary in different cultures, they can cause difficulties in understanding and translation. For an adequate translation, it is essential to grasp the context, especially the extralinguistic context. It can be argued that this is a reason why in an audiovisual project color alone can have no significant effect in evoking a desired emotion by the audiovisual producer (Nie, 2021). Color, as well as camera movements and editing techniques, are preconceived and stereotyped devices that audiovisual producers use to control attention and filter the information available to the audience throughout the narrative of an audiovisual project (Carroll & Seeley, 2013). In this sense, Noël Carroll and William Seeley (2013) argue that audiovisual projects can be considered attention management tools intentionally designed to direct the viewer's attention towards the perceptual characteristics that have artistically been highlighted by the audiovisual producer. A director's creative decisions come from the intention he or she wishes to communicate (Carroll & Seeley, 2013). These creative decisions can be camera shots, editing, soundtrack, and color in production design. Nonetheless, this does not mean that creative decisions, like S the use of color in an audiovisual project, translate properly without the context intended for them, as seen S in the present research. Previous literature reviews have suggested that pastel colors can evoke softer emotional responses (Casas & Chinoperekweyi, 2019; Mulyati &E Exposto, 2023). However, in our study, we did not observe these differences to be statistically signRificant. While many publications discuss the potential emotional impact of color on audiences, few have examined this topic using a quantitative and P experimental approach with full control over confounding variables. In our design, participants viewed the same emotionally charged narrative under two diffNerent color conditions: pastel and saturated. Our goal was not to create ‘pure’ emotional stimuli, but to explore how pastel versus saturated colors influenced the I perceived intensity of the dominant emotion, while also examining the presence and intensity of secondary emotions. The finding that emotional conteEnt had a stronger influence on viewers’ perceptions than the color treatment aligns with previous reseLarch. For instance, Andreu-Sánchez et al. (2021) concluded that, in some cases, narrative content exerts a greater emotional impact than formal elements such as C cinematography or design choices. They suggested that the scriptwriter may hold more influence over I viewers’ emotional responses than directors of photography, producers, or creative designers. This T interpretation enriches the discussion and provides valuable insights for future studies exploring the relative R impact of form and content in audiovisual media. So, since pastel color alone in audiovisuals may not be a strong determinant of emAotional response, future research could explore additional contexts in which pastel tones might influence viewers’ affective reactions —such as educational videos, branding and marketing contexts, or different narrative genres. Limitations The main limitation of our work is that, while our stimuli were carefully designed and revised based on expert feedback and two rounds of pre-testing, they were not drawn from previously validated emotional video sets. This may limit the generalizability and emotional strength of the stimuli. For instance, the mean rating for happiness was relatively low (2.8 on a 5-point Likert scale), suggesting that the intended emotion was not strongly elicited in all cases. Such variability in emotional intensity could have moderated the potential effects of color on emotional perception, possibly dampening any differences between pastel and saturated versions. Future research would benefit from further refining custom stimuli to achieve stronger and more consistent emotional responses. Including physiological or behavioral measures in addition to self-reports could also help confirm the effectiveness of emotional elicitation. Future works should consider these limitations. Another limitation of our work is not having asked exact age to participants to be able to present the mean, the standard deviation, minimum, and maximum levels rather than the frequency distribution of age. Related to this, a limitation that might have influence this study is the fact that the most common age of our study respondent is in the 18-24 age bracket. In contrast to younger individuals who favor bold and bright colors, middle-aged and older populations tend to prefer pastel tones (Hunjet & Vuk, ARTICLE IN PRESS 2017). This statement correlates with the findings of Kurt and Osueke (2014) study regarding the effects of color on the mood of college students. In their finding, the least favorite color preferred by the respondents were pastel colors pink and grey (Kurt & Osueke, 2014). Our study was conducted with a specific sample size and demographic, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to broader populations. Also, cultural differences in color perception and emotional response could also affect the outcomes, and these were not accounted for in the study. Besides that, individual differences in color perception, such as color vision deficiencies or personal associations with certain colors, were not accounted for, which could have influenced the results. So, given that previous experiences influence people’s preferences, as proposed by the Ecological Valence Theory (Palmer & Schloss, 2010), a more culturally diverse sample would have benefited this study. Another limitation is that the questionnaires allowed participants to finish their participation without having answered the 100% of the questions. In future works this should be avoided. Also, the study specifically compared pastel and saturated colors, which may not cover the full spectrum of color's impact on emotion. Other color variations, such as monochromatic or complementary color schemes, were not explored and could yield different results. Another limitation is that the measurement of the affective experience was based on categorical approach and other core dimensions such as valence or arousal could have been included in the study. An additional limitation of this study is the absence of post S hoc correction (as Bonferroni correction or other methods) to control for multiple comparisons. Our primary S goal was to explore potential trends in how pastel and saturated colors influence emotional responses rather than to strictly control for family-wise error rate in a confirmatoryE hypothesis-testing framework. Given the exploratory nature of this work and the relatively limited numRber of comparisons, we decided not to apply Bonferroni corrections, which, while effective in reducing Type I errors, can be overly conservative and P substantially increase the risk of Type II errors (i.e., overlooking potentially meaningful effects). Nonetheless, we acknowledge that this approach iNncreases the likelihood of false positives, and future confirmatory studies should employ appropriate multiple-comparison corrections to ensure robust I replication. Additionally, future studies with larger and more diverse stimulus sets could examine whether the observed trends hold under more stringenEt statistical controls and across different experimental designs. In addition, this study focused on six basiLc emotions: disgust, anger, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise. Human emotions are nuanced and varied, and the selected emotions may not fully represent the range of C emotional responses that color can evoke. I T Conclusion R We conclude that pastel color in audiovisual project does not significantly influence, on its own, viewers’ emotional perception. DAespite its characteristic of being a soft color, pastel color does not significantly evoke emotions with less intensity than saturated colors. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of how pastel colors in audiovisual content can influence emotional responses, although their impact may be limited without the support of other cinematic elements. JSON: Name: pastel_color_emotion_experiment Title: Randomized between-subjects experimental assessment of pastel versus saturated color production on viewers' perceived basic emotions in short audiovisual narratives Short Hypothesis: Short audiovisual scenes produced with pastel color palettes cause lower self-reported intensity ratings for basic emotions (disgust, anger, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise) than otherwise-matched scenes produced with saturated color palettes. Related Work: Prior work has examined links between color properties (hue, saturation, brightness) and affect, and separate lines of audiovisual research have measured how cinematographic elements (lighting, music, editing) alter viewers' emotions. Existing experimental approaches typically compare saturated color versus grayscale, vary hue, or manipulate saturation in still images or isolated clips, and often use small or convenience samples and single-modality self-reports. Limitations in the literature include: limited control of production confounds (music, shot composition, acting), lack of matched paired productions that differ only in saturation, scarcity of studies focused specifically on pastel (low chroma, high luminance) palettes, reliance on self-report without physiological or behavioral corroboration, inconsistent statistical controls for multiple comparisons, and narrow demographic sampling. These gaps leave unresolved whether pastel tones alone, when embedded in controlled audiovisual narratives, modulate viewers' emotional intensity in a reproducible manner. Abstract: This research pipeline addresses whether pastel color palettes, independent of other production factors, modulate viewers' perception of basic emotions in short audiovisual narratives. We propose a randomized between-subjects experimental design that uses paired, matched filmlets differing only in color saturation (pastel vs saturated). Participants will rate the intensity of six basic emotions and continuous affective dimensions (valence, arousal); optional physiological measures (skin conductance, pupil diameter) will be collected in laboratory subsamples. The main contribution is a controlled, pre-registered test of the causal effect of pastel saturation on emotional intensity using mixed-effects modeling and corrected hypothesis testing. Expected outcomes are precise effect-size estimates for saturation-driven differences across emotions and boundary conditions (e.g., with/without music). Results will clarify whether pastel palettes are sufficient to attenuate or alter affective responses and will guide audiovisual practice and future experimental research on color-emotion interactions. Experiments: Datasets: primary dataset = 12 paired 30-second filmlets (six target emotions, each with pastel and saturated versions) produced with identical script, acting, framing, lighting intent, and duration; secondary validation dataset = a set of validated emotional film clips (for benchmarking). Participants: online sample N>=600 (balanced by condition) and lab subsample N>=120 for physiological recording. Randomization: participants randomized to one color condition (pastel or saturated); within each condition, filmlet order randomized. Baselines: saturated-color condition and grayscale condition (additional arm) and validated film-clip benchmark. Measures: self-reported intensity for six basic emotions on 1–5 Likert scales, continuous valence and arousal ratings (e.g., 9-point SAM-like scale), response time to emotion selection, and physiological signals (skin conductance, pupilometry, optional heart-rate variability) in lab. Evaluation metrics: mean differences, Cohen's d, rank-biserial correlation, mixed-effects linear models with fixed effects (color condition, target emotion, music presence) and random intercepts for participant and stimulus; MANOVA as secondary check; Bayes factors for null vs alternative. Statistical controls: false discovery rate (Benjamini-Hochberg) across multiple emotion tests and pre-registered primary endpoints. Power analysis: target power 0.9 to detect d=0.25 requires ~392 participants; online N>=600 allows subgroup analyses. Experimental setup: pretest stimuli validation (≥85% target-emotion recognition), mandatory completion QA, exclusion of color-vision-deficient participants, demographic collection (age, gender, culture). Ablation studies: (1) music on vs music off, (2) production-phase color design vs postproduction color-grading, (3) within-subject cross-over (subset) vs between-subject-only design, (4) addition of grayscale baseline. Analysis plan: primary test = mixed-effects model contrast of pastel vs saturated on target-emotion intensity; secondary tests = interaction effects with music, participant age group, and culture; report corrected p-values, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and Bayes factors; perform sensitivity analyses excluding low-engagement respondents. Risk Factors and Limitations: Small or null effect sizes: pastel vs saturated differences may be very small, requiring large samples to detect; multiple comparisons inflate false-positive risk if not corrected. Stimulus validity: ensuring matched stimuli that differ only in saturation is technically challenging; inadvertent differences in lighting, contrast, or actor performance can confound results. Measurement biases: reliance on self-report is prone to demand characteristics and social desirability; physiological measures add cost and may have low signal-to-noise. Sampling bias: online convenience samples may not generalize across cultures or age groups; cultural differences in color semantics may mask or reverse effects. Missing data and attrition: partial completions reduce effective sample size. Color perception variability: color vision deficiencies and display calibration differences (participant screens) will introduce uncontrolled variance in online data. Scalability and compute: processing and synchronizing physiological signals for large lab cohorts require specialized equipment and expertise. Statistical concerns: family-wise error control and pre-registration are required to avoid p-hacking; post-hoc exploration must be clearly labeled. External validity: findings from short, scripted filmlets may not generalize to longer-form narrative media, advertising, or interactive media.
